title: Will the U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal Proceed?
gist: CSIS senior adviser and former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney analyzes the July 22, 2026 U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement, noting Saudi Arabia burns more than a third of its domestic electricity generation as crude it would rather export, making nuclear a rational Vision 2030 play. He argues Trump's day-later insistence that the deal is contingent on Saudi normalization with Israel is unworkable — Riyadh still requires a Palestinian state that Israel has ruled out — and that Trump has already given the Saudis F-35s, AI and economic deals and now civil nuclear without normalization, leaving Congress's 90-day review and U.S. reliability in doubt.

insights.claim: On July 22, 2026 the United States and Saudi Arabia signed a bilateral agreement laying the foundation for civil nuclear cooperation, including commercial development of a Saudi nuclear power industry using U.S. technology.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Opens a potentially large addressable market for U.S. nuclear vendors and EPC contractors — but only if the deal survives its political conditions.
insights.locator: On July 22, the United States and Saudi Arabia signed

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia currently generates more than a third of its domestic electricity by burning crude oil it would rather export for profit, which alongside solar and wind makes nuclear power a rational Vision 2030 diversification ambition rather than a proliferation pretext.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Quantifies the economic driver: every megawatt of Saudi nuclear or renewables frees crude for export, so Saudi power-sector buildout is directly export-volume accretive.
insights.quote: for a country that currently generates more than a third of its domestic electricity by burning crude oil that it would rather export for profit, nuclear power is not an unreasonable ambition
insights.locator: Along with solar and wind, Saudi Arabia regards nuclear energy

insights.claim: Press reports suggest the agreement would permit Saudi Arabia to develop uranium enrichment capacity, which would put it on the short list of countries — currently just 14 — with indigenous nuclear enrichment facilities.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The '14 countries' benchmark shows how exceptional the concession would be and why it drew immediate proliferation objections.
insights.quote: the short list of countries—currently just 14—with indigenous nuclear enrichment facilities
insights.locator: The first was press reports suggesting

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia reportedly has considerable uranium deposits and has long had ambitions to own the entire nuclear supply chain from uranium mine to power plant.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals Saudi intent to build a domestic nuclear fuel-cycle industry, not just import reactors — a wider procurement and mining opportunity if permitted.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia reportedly has considerable uranium deposits

insights.claim: Even under the reported terms, enrichment would come only after a multiyear period of consultations over the commercial viability of a facility, yet the mere prospect raised proliferation concerns in the United States and Israel that Saudi Arabia could be put on a path to nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The political blowback vastly outran the practical timeline — a reminder that headline risk on this deal is driven by optics, not near-term capability.
insights.locator: Although such a development would, according to these press reports

insights.claim: Ruling out enrichment may vex Saudi leadership because even if such a facility would be extraordinarily expensive, take a decade or more, and prove commercially unviable, Riyadh saw great political value in claiming both the right and the ability to pursue it.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Saudi interest in enrichment is a status and leverage play rather than an economic project — so the sticking point is symbolic and therefore hard to negotiate away.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia likely discerned great political value in claiming both the right and ability to pursue it.
insights.locator: Beyond that, ruling out enrichment may also vex the Saudi leadership

insights.claim: Not a day after the agreement was signed, President Trump issued a social media statement linking the deal to Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords, seemed to rule out uranium enrichment, and oddly appeared to equate the Iranian and UAE nuclear programs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Terms of major U.S. bilateral agreements can be rewritten by a single presidential post within 24 hours — a discount factor to apply to all such announcements.
insights.locator: The second controversy came seemingly in reaction to the first

insights.claim: Trump's condition surprised many observers because it added a major requirement to an agreement his most senior officials had negotiated on his behalf and signed to great fanfare only a day earlier.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signed-official-level agreements are not reliable endpoints in this administration — a process risk for anyone underwriting U.S. bilateral commitments.
insights.locator: Trump’s insistence that the nuclear deal would be contingent

insights.claim: The nuclear deal does not change the Saudi calculus on normalization: since negotiations began under the Biden administration, Saudi agreement has depended on Israel supporting the creation of a Palestinian state, which the current Israeli government has explicitly and repeatedly ruled out.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The attached condition is effectively unmeetable, so treat Saudi normalization — and by extension deal completion — as off the table near term.
insights.quote: A Palestinian state has been explicitly and repeatedly ruled out by the current Israeli government.
insights.locator: This nuclear deal does not change the Saudi calculus

insights.claim: Trump's move was likely aimed at blunting the domestic and Israeli criticism that emerged when the deal was announced, but it leaves the Saudis, the U.S. nuclear power industry and the U.S. Congress — which has 90 days to review the deal — quite confused.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 90-day congressional review clock is the concrete date to watch, and U.S. nuclear industry planning is now operating without clarity on terms.
insights.quote: it will leave everyone—including the Saudis, the U.S. nuclear power industry, and the U.S. Congress, which has 90 days to review the deal—quite confused

insights.claim: The Biden-era U.S.-Saudi grand deal was designed as a package — a mutual defense treaty, a bilateral defense cooperation agreement, advancement of Palestinian statehood prospects, and economic measures including civil nuclear cooperation — precisely because only something for everyone could reach the 67 Senate votes needed to ratify a U.S.-Saudi treaty.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explains why a treaty-grade U.S.-Saudi security guarantee remains out of reach: the 67-vote threshold requires a Palestinian component nobody can deliver.
insights.quote: only a deal with something for everyone—the United States, Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the Palestinians—could garner the 67 votes necessary in the U.S. Senate to win ratification of a U.S.-Saudi treaty

insights.claim: The Gaza war following the October 7 terror attacks and Israel's refusal to support a two-state solution effectively took the U.S.-Saudi grand bargain off the table for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The collapse of the package deal is structural, not tactical — do not expect a comprehensive U.S.-Saudi-Israel settlement in this cycle.
insights.locator: The Gaza war in the aftermath of the October 7 terror attacks

insights.claim: Trump has already given Saudi Arabia most of what normalization would have bought — a major strategic partnership upgrade including an agreement to sell F-35 fighter jets, economic agreements including on artificial intelligence, and now civil nuclear cooperation — all without Saudi normalization with Israel, which effectively leaves normalization even more remote.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The core analytical insight: Saudi Arabia has been paid in advance, destroying U.S. leverage over normalization — abandon trades premised on an eventual Saudi-Israel accord.
insights.quote: And he did it all without Saudi Arabia normalizing with Israel, which effectively left the prospect of normalization even more remote.

insights.claim: By inserting normalization at the last minute, Trump throws a great deal of uncertainty into an already controversial deal and creates more questions about the reliability of the United States as a strategic partner.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: U.S. counterparty reliability is the second-order casualty, which pushes Gulf states toward diversified suppliers of technology, arms and nuclear capability.
insights.quote: creates more questions about the reliability of the United States as a strategic partner
insights.locator: By inserting normalization at the last minute
